rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-3 - own case study (Senyera WUA, Valencia), hydraulic model calibrated with five pressure sensors and intake flow meters (relative pressure error +2.8%), GA optimisation of intake grouping, 12 scenarios compared with 2006 energy data (Tables 4-9).
rows.notes: The study reports only energy consumption and energy cost results (e.g. predicted 36.4% energy saving, Table 8; annual saving 29,484 kWh, Table 9). It schedules all sectors in fixed 2 h periods (TPer = 2 h) but never measures or models whether plots receive more or less water than required, crop water requirements, or water-use efficiency. The claimed effect (inefficient water management from uniform irrigation times) is a statement of the citing review, not a finding of this study.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-3 - own case study with calibrated EPANET/HuraGIS model, GA sectoring, 12 scenarios and comparison with 2006 measured energy consumption (Tables 4-9).
rows.notes: The passage describes an improved method (intakes not restricted to fixed time periods, crop water requirements satisfied more efficiently) that is not the one tested here: this study groups intakes into sectors that operate in fixed 2 h periods and optimises only energy (WPD). No result on satisfaction of crop water requirements or water conservation is reported; the only outputs are energy and cost indicators. The study is the predecessor methodology that the review says was later improved.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is an energy-optimisation case study (GA + calibrated hydraulic model) for one small WUA; it contains no water-application or crop-water-requirement results, so neither water_conservation claim is supported by its own evidence. The authors themselves note the WUA is small and results are difficult to extrapolate to other schemes (Section 3.3).
